claims.text: The baseline alloy is equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn, corresponding to approximately 20 at.% of each element.
The baseline alloy has a homogeneous microstructure and an initially oxide-free surface.
Approximately 6 at.% Mo or W can replace Mn, reducing Mn from 20 at.% to about 14 at.%.
The proposed Mo or W substitution can be made while preserving overall phase stability.
The comparison should expose baseline and modified alloys to identical oxygen-rich conditions at 900–1200 °C for tens to hundreds of hours.
In equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn, initial oxidation behavior follows atomic-size and redox-potential effects, with redox potential becoming dominant over time and causing composition inversion.
Oxidation of the modified alloy will evolve from an initially nucleated, compositionally graded oxide into a continuous and adherent protective film.
Mo and W have a higher relevant redox potential than the Mn they replace.
The higher redox potential of Mo or W makes the dopant preferentially resist oxidation and alter early oxide nucleation.
Mo or W substitution will reduce compositional inversion at the oxide/alloy interface.
A continuous, compact, adherent protective scale suppresses inward oxygen diffusion and outward metal-cation transport.
Mo- or W-modified CoCrFeNiMn will have a slower oxide-scale growth rate than equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn under identical exposure conditions.
Mo- or W-modified CoCrFeNiMn will exhibit less compositional inversion at the oxide/alloy interface than the baseline alloy.
Atom probe tomography and X-ray absorption spectroscopy can characterize oxidation-induced composition profiles, oxidation states, and oxide-structure evolution in CoCrFeNiMn.
The hypothesized behavior should hold throughout 900–1200 °C in oxygen-rich environments.
The hypothesized behavior is restricted to dopant concentrations that preserve phase stability and avoid significant non-oxidation-related microstructural changes.
Dopant-induced changes in phase stability or microstructural evolution could confound attribution of oxidation behavior to redox potential.
The optimum Mo or W concentration for slowing oxidation without degrading other properties is unknown.
The baseline and modified alloys constitute a controlled comparison when tested under identical temperature, atmosphere, and duration.
Failure of the modified alloy to show both statistically slower scale growth and reduced interface inversion relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
